To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. pulse pressure is an independent risk factor for myocardial infraction in the general population; 2. the relation between pulse pressure and the incidence of myocardinal infarction is curvilinear; 3. the incidence of myocardinfarction is highest in those individuals with the lowest pulse pressure and the highest in those with the highest pulse pressure; 4. the lowest pulse pressure is associated with the greatest risk reduction with antihypertensive treatment.

(a) a high diastolic blood pres-sure is associated with an increased risk for myocardial infa-rction; (b) the association is not linear but is J-shaped (i.e., the risk for myocardial in-farction increases with decreasing diastolic blood pressures); (c) the association is independent of other risk factors; and (d) the association is more pronounced among persons with high pulse pressure.

(1) pulse pressure is a better predictor of myocardial infac-tion risk than mean arterial pressure and (2) the relationship of pulse pressure to risk is J-shaped, with the lowest risk in subjects with pulse pressures of 50-59 mm Hg.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hemodynamic mechanisms that may explain the J-shaped curve.
the relation between pulse pressure, mean pressure, and the backward pressure wave.
the study of the pulsatile arterial hemodynamic and its influence on coronary hemodynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the J-shaped curve between pulse pressure and myocardial infarctions is probably due to the fact that pulse pressure is a marker of a backward wave, the amplitude of which is dependent on the length of the arterial vasculature and on the distance between the aorta and reflection sites.

pulse pressure is an independent predictor of coronary events, but that the predictive value of pulse pressure should be considered as an index of arterial hemodynamics rather than a simple measure of arterial stiffness.
a higher pulse pressure, as a result of an increased backward pressure wave, may be a marker for an increased cardiovascular risk, but it does not represent a causal mechanism for coronary events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pulse pressure, as a measure of arterial distensibility, is a useful marker of cardiovascular risk.
pulse pressure is a marker of cardiovascular risk, but it is not a cause of myocardial infacction.
the risk of myocardia1 infarction is related not only to mean arterial pressure but also to the magnitude of the pulse pressure and to the distance between the aorta and the coronary arteries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between pulse pressure and the risk for cardiovascular disease is not linear.
pulse pressure is a better predictor of myocardial infraction than diastolic pressure.
pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure are equally important determinants of myocardial infraction.
